questions.prompt:
A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m.
(a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
(b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2)
(c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution:
(a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. [M1 A1]
(b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. [M1 A1]
(c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [B1 B1 B1]

questions.prompt: Express the units of energy and of pressure in SI base units. (2)
questions.solution:
Energy: kg m² s⁻² [B1]
Pressure: kg m⁻¹ s⁻² [B1]

questions.prompt: Estimate the order of magnitude of the kinetic energy of a family car on a motorway. (2)
questions.solution:
½ × 1000 × 30² = 4.5 × 10⁵ J [M1]
Order of magnitude 10⁵–10⁶ J [A1]

questions.prompt: Write 0.47 μF in farads and 3.3 MΩ in ohms, in standard form. (2)
Diameter readings of a putty cylinder are 30.5, 30.2, 29.1, 29.6 and 30.1 mm. Show that the percentage uncertainty in the mean diameter is about 2.3%. (3)
The cylinder has length (65 ± 2) mm and diameter 29.9 mm ± 2.3%. Calculate its volume and the absolute uncertainty in the volume. (4)

A sound pulse takes 0.18 ms to travel along a 0.900 m steel rod.
(i) Calculate the speed of sound in steel. (2)
(ii) State which oscilloscope control centres the trace vertically. (1)
Explain why doubling the length of the rod gives a more accurate speed of sound. (2)
questions.solution:
Time doubles while the reading uncertainty stays the same [B1]
Percentage uncertainty in time is halved [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to avoid parallax error when reading a pin's position against a ruler behind it. (2)
questions.solution:
Place eye level with the pin, perpendicular to the ruler [B1]
Use a set square / mirror to line up the pin with the scale [B1]

questions.prompt: In ρ = RA/L, diameter is measured to 2%, R to 1% and L to 0.5%. Find the total uncertainty and the largest contributor. (2)
questions.solution:
1 + 4 + 0.5 = 5.5% [B1]
Diameter contributes most [B1]

questions.prompt: State the quantity given by the area under a force-time graph and its unit in base units. (2)
questions.solution:
Impulse / change in momentum [B1]
kg m s⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: Estimate the take-off speed of a high jumper whose centre of mass rises 1.0 m. (2)
Classify momentum, energy and power as scalar or vector. (1)
questions.solution: Momentum is a vector; energy and power are scalars [B1]

questions.prompt: A protractor reads an angle of 25° to the nearest 1°, with both arms read. Estimate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
questions.solution:
Absolute uncertainty about ±1° [B1]
4% [B1]

questions.prompt: A stroboscope's flashes last up to 300 μs at up to 150 Hz. Calculate the maximum duty cycle and explain why short flashes are needed. (2)
questions.solution:
300 × 10⁻⁶ × 150 = 0.045 [B1]
Short flashes freeze the motion without blurring [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why decay data are plotted on a logarithmic scale. (1)
questions.solution: Exponential decay gives a straight line, making the decay constant easy to find [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the rms speed of molecules in air at 105 kPa and density 1.25 kg m⁻³, to an appropriate number of significant figures. (2)
A trace shows two signals with the same frequency, offset by a quarter of a cycle. State the phase difference in radians and degrees. (2)
Suggest why dental X-rays are only taken when a problem is reported. (2)
questions.solution:
X-rays are ionising and can damage cells / cause cancer [B1]
Only justified when the diagnostic benefit outweighs the risk [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to compare lengths such as 10⁻¹⁹ Gm and 10⁷ fm. (1)
questions.solution: 10⁻¹⁰ m and 10⁻⁸ m, so 10⁻¹⁹ Gm is shorter [B1]

questions.prompt: State what the gradient and area of a velocity-time graph represent. (2)
questions.solution:
Gradient = acceleration [B1]
Area = displacement [B1]

questions.prompt:
Electromagnetic radiation has frequency $5\times10^{14}$ Hz.
(a) Calculate its wavelength in vacuum. (2)
(b) Calculate the energy of one photon using $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s. (2)
(c) Explain what is meant by diffraction and state when it is most noticeable. (3)
questions.solution:
(a) $\lambda=c/f=6.000\times10^{-7}$ m. [M1 A1]
(b) $E=hf=3.315\times10^{-19}$ J. [M1 A1]
(c) Diffraction is spreading of waves at an aperture/edge and is greatest when the aperture size is comparable with the wavelength. [B1 B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
Rubidium has isotopes ⁸⁵₃₇Rb and ⁸⁷₃₇Rb.
(i) State how the nuclei of the two isotopes differ. (1)
(ii) ⁹⁰₃₈Sr decays by β⁻ emission to an isotope of yttrium. State the nucleon number and proton number of the yttrium nucleus. (1)
(iii) ⁴⁰₁₉K can decay by electron capture to argon. State two differences between the constituents of the potassium and argon nuclei. (2)
hints: Electron capture turns p into n.
questions.solution:
(i) ⁸⁷Rb has two more neutrons [B1]
(ii) Nucleon number 90, proton number 39 [B1]
(iii) Argon has one fewer proton [B1]
and one more neutron [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare electron capture with β⁺ decay in terms of the particles involved and emitted. (3)
questions.solution:
In both a proton changes into a neutron [B1]
Electron capture absorbs an inner-shell electron; β⁺ emits a positron [B1]
Both emit an electron neutrino (electron capture is followed by X-ray emission as electrons fill the vacancy) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Write the equation for the alpha decay of ²³⁸₉₂U to thorium. (2)
(ii) Tritium ³₁H decays by β⁻ to ³₂He. Name the exchange particle and explain why it must be this particle. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th [B1]
+ ⁴₂He [B1]
(ii) W⁻ boson [B1]
Weak interaction; it carries negative charge from the neutron side to the electron [B1]

questions.prompt:
A dark line in the Sun's spectrum has wavelength 589 nm.
(i) Calculate the energy change of an electron in eV for this transition. (3)
(ii) Explain the difference between emission and absorption line spectra in terms of atomic processes. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 589 × 10⁻⁹ [M1]
= 3.38 × 10⁻¹⁹ J [M1]
= 2.11 eV [A1]
(ii) Absorption: electrons absorb photons of exactly the energy difference and are excited [B1]
These wavelengths are missing from continuous light passing through cool gas [B1]
Emission: excited electrons de-excite emitting photons of specific wavelengths, giving bright lines [B1]

questions.prompt:
Carbon-14 decays: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + β⁻ + ν̄ₑ.
(i) State the quark change. (1)
(ii) Explain how the continuous energy spectrum of the β⁻ particles supports the existence of the antineutrino. (2)
(iii) An antineutrino interacts with a proton: ν̄ₑ + p → e⁺ + X. Identify X. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Down quark changes to up quark [B1]
(ii) If only two products, β⁻ would always have the same energy [B1]
A third particle shares the energy, giving a range [B1]
(iii) Neutron [B1]

questions.prompt: A positron annihilates with an electron, both effectively at rest. Gamma photons of energy 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J and 1.2 × 10⁻¹³ J are detected. Deduce which could come from this annihilation. (3)
questions.solution:
Rest energy of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² [M1]
= 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J; two photons each of this energy [M1]
So the 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J photon [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm. (2)
Light of photon energy 3.5 eV falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in J. (2)
Calculate the specific charge of a ⁷₃Li nucleus (take mass = 7 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). (2)
Explain why K⁻ → π⁻ + π⁰ is a weak interaction. (2)
questions.solution:
K⁻ has strangeness −1; pions have strangeness 0 [B1]
Strangeness changes, so it must be weak [B1]

questions.prompt: Photoelectrons have a stopping potential of 0.80 V. State their maximum kinetic energy in eV and in J. (2)
A proton and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Compare their speeds. (2)
questions.solution:
Same momentum [B1]
Electron speed is about 1840 times greater [B1]

questions.prompt:
Electrons at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ have wavelength 3.6 × 10⁻¹¹ m, and at 4.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ have 1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
(i) Show the data fit λ ∝ 1/v. (2)
(ii) Calculate the Planck constant suggested. (2)

Electrons pass through graphite onto a fluorescent screen.
(i) Explain how the rings support a wave model. (2)
(ii) Explain how light from the screen shows particle behaviour. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Rings are a diffraction pattern [B1]
Diffraction is a wave property; λ comparable to atomic spacing [B1]
(ii) Each electron gives up its energy at a single point, producing a flash [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give the quark composition of the Λ⁰ (strangeness −1). (1)
(ii) Λ⁰ → π⁰ + n. Name the interaction and explain. (2)
(iii) Identify X in Λ̄⁰ → π⁰ + X. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) uds [B1]
(ii) Weak interaction [B1]
Strangeness changes from −1 to 0 [B1]
(iii) Antineutron [B1]

questions.prompt: The rest energy of a particle equals the energy of a photon of frequency 2.70 × 10²³ Hz. Calculate it in MeV. (2)
A muon (rest energy 106 MeV) and antimuon annihilate at rest. Calculate the minimum frequency of each photon. (2)
An atom has electrons excited to the fourth energy level. State how many different wavelengths can be emitted. (2)
Calculate the specific charge of a ¹⁹F⁻ ion (mass 19 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). (2)
State two properties of a muon. (2)
questions.solution:
A lepton with charge −1 [B1]
About 200 times the electron mass; decays to an electron [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the maximum speed of photoelectrons with maximum kinetic energy 1.5 eV. (2)
In β⁻ decay, explain which lepton accompanies the electron and why. (2)
questions.solution:
Electron antineutrino [B1]
Conserves lepton number (0 = 1 − 1) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the four fundamental interactions. (1)
(ii) State the products of free neutron decay and the interaction responsible. (2)
(iii) Name the exchange particle when two electrons repel. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Strong, weak, electromagnetic, gravitational [B1]
(ii) Proton, electron and electron antineutrino [B1]
Weak interaction (quark changes flavour) [B1]
(iii) Virtual photon [B1]

questions.prompt: Classify π⁺, n, K⁺ and Σ⁰ as baryon or meson, and state which are hadrons. (2)
questions.solution:
Baryons: n, Σ⁰; mesons: π⁺, K⁺ [B1]
All four are hadrons [B1]

questions.prompt: In π⁰ → γ + e⁺ + e⁻, compare the rest energy of the π⁰ with the products and explain what happens to the difference. (2)
questions.solution:
π⁰ rest energy (135 MeV) is much greater than 2 × 0.51 MeV [B1]
Difference becomes photon energy and kinetic energy [B1]

questions.prompt: An electron and a proton travel at the same speed. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths. (2)
Explain the effect on maximum kinetic energy and photocurrent of increasing frequency at constant intensity. (2)
questions.solution:
Maximum kinetic energy increases [B1]
Fewer photons per second, so current decreases slightly [B1]

questions.prompt:
Potassium-40 (Z = 19) decays by electron capture, then emits a single 1.46 MeV gamma photon.
(i) Write the decay equation. (2)
(ii) Name the interaction responsible. (1)
(iii) Calculate the photon wavelength. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ⁴⁰₁₉K + ⁰₋₁e → ⁴⁰₁₈Ar [B1]
+ νₑ [B1]
(ii) Weak interaction [B1]
(iii) E = 1.46 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 2.34 × 10⁻¹³ J [M1]
λ = 8.5 × 10⁻¹³ m [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the speed of an electron with the same de Broglie wavelength as a proton moving at 2.8 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹. (2)
A cosmic-ray nucleus has mass 8.02 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and specific charge 4.39 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Find its neutron number. (3)
The nucleus (8.02 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) has kinetic energy 215 MeV. Calculate its speed, ignoring relativity. (3)

(i) Show how conservation laws apply to π⁺ → e⁺ + νₑ. (2)
(ii) Explain the strangeness change in K⁺ → μ⁺ + ν_μ. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Charge: +1 = +1 + 0 [B1]
Lepton number: 0 = −1 + 1; baryon number 0 = 0 [B1]
(ii) K⁺ has strangeness +1; products have 0 [B1]
Strangeness isn't conserved, so it must be a weak decay [B1]

questions.prompt: 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J photons release electrons with maximum speed 4.2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Calculate the work function. (2)
A titanium ion (Z = 22, fully ionised) has specific charge 4.8 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Find its neutron number. (2)
Describe the quark change and exchange particle in electron capture. (2)
questions.solution:
u → d (uud → udd), with an electron neutrino emitted [B1]
Exchange particle is a W⁺ boson [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the maximum speed of electrons accelerated through 130 V. (2)
Hydrogen atoms are excited by 12.74 eV photons. How many photon frequencies can then be emitted? (2)
questions.solution:
12.74 eV raises atoms to n = 4 [M1]
6 frequencies [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an alpha particle (6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 4.5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. (1)

A rain sensor sends light into a windscreen (n = 1.50) so that it meets the outer surface at 45°.
(i) Show by calculation that the light is totally internally reflected when the screen is dry. (2)
(ii) Explain, with a calculation, why a water droplet (n = 1.33) on the outer surface reduces the light reaching the detector. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) sin C = 1/1.50, C = 41.8° [M1]
45° > C so TIR occurs [A1]
(ii) Critical angle glass–water: sin C = 1.33/1.50, C = 62.5° [M1]
45° < 62.5° so light refracts into the water and less is reflected to the detector [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a small variation in the refractive index across the thickness of the glass could affect the path of the ray. (2)
questions.solution:
Ray refracts slightly at each change in n / follows a curved path [B1]
Angle at the surface could change, affecting whether TIR occurs [B1]

questions.prompt:
White light passes through a green filter then a single slit onto a screen.
(i) Describe the pattern. (2)
(ii) Describe how the pattern changes when a red filter is used. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Wide bright central maximum [B1]
Narrower, dimmer subsidiary maxima either side [B1]
(ii) Maxima become wider / more spread out [B1]
Because red has a longer wavelength [B1]

questions.prompt:
Green light of wavelength 520 nm falls normally on a grating with 400 lines per mm.
(i) Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. (2)
(ii) The filter actually transmits 500–540 nm. Suggest how this affects the maxima. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) d = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = 520 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ [M1]
θ = 12.0° [A1]
(ii) Each maximum becomes a band / broader [B1]
Spread increases with order (first order ≈ 11.5° to 12.5°) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Light passes from glass A (n = 1.60) into glass B (n = 1.45) at an angle of incidence of 50°.
(i) Calculate the angle of refraction. (2)
(ii) Explain how the path shows that n of A is greater than n of B. (1)
hints: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
questions.solution:
(i) sin r = 1.60 sin 50° ÷ 1.45 = 0.845 [M1]
r = 57.7° [A1]
(ii) Ray bends away from the normal entering B [B1]

questions.prompt: A string's fundamental frequency is 110 Hz. State the frequencies of the second and third harmonics and the number of nodes for the third harmonic. (2)
questions.solution:
220 Hz and 330 Hz [B1]
4 nodes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect on fringe spacing of halving the slit separation and using red light instead of blue. (2)
questions.solution:
Halving s doubles w [B1]
Longer wavelength increases w further [B1]

questions.prompt: State the type of wave produced by a loudspeaker and describe the motion of air particles. (2)
questions.solution:
Longitudinal [B1]
Particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions [B1]

questions.prompt: Light of wavelength 550 nm falls on a grating with 600 lines per mm. Calculate the total number of maxima seen. (3)
questions.solution:
d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m [M1]
d/λ = 3.03, so highest order 3 [M1]
7 maxima [A1]

questions.prompt: State the conditions for observable two-source interference. (2)
questions.solution:
Coherent sources – same frequency, constant phase difference [B1]
Similar amplitudes for clear minima [B1]

questions.prompt: Two pendulums of periods 2.00 s and 2.05 s start in phase. Explain why they are in antiphase after about 41 s. (2)
questions.solution:
One gains 0.05 s per oscillation on the other [B1]
Half a period (1 s) gained after about 20 oscillations ≈ 41 s [B1]

questions.prompt: A wave has speed 340 m s⁻¹ and frequency 850 Hz. Calculate the phase difference between points 0.10 m apart. (2)
questions.solution:
λ = 0.40 m [M1]
Δφ = π/2 rad [A1]

questions.prompt: A fibre core has n = 1.48 and cladding n = 1.46. Calculate the critical angle and explain why cladding is used. (3)
questions.solution:
sin C = 1.46 ÷ 1.48 [M1]
C = 80.6° [A1]
Cladding protects the core and prevents signal crossover / reduces modal dispersion [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why polarisation is evidence that light is a transverse wave. (2)
questions.solution:
Only transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to propagation that can be restricted to one plane [B1]
Light can be polarised by a filter [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a stationary wave forms when a violin string is plucked. (3)
questions.solution:
Waves travel along the string and reflect at the fixed ends [B1]
Waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose [B1]
Nodes at the ends and an antinode in the middle (first harmonic) [B1]

questions.prompt:
A 0.30 m string under 30 N tension vibrates at 400 Hz in its first harmonic.
(i) Calculate the wave speed. (1)
(ii) Calculate the mass per unit length. (2)
The tension of a string is increased by 21%. Calculate the percentage change in its fundamental frequency. (2)
questions.solution:
f increases by √1.21 = 1.10 [M1]
10% increase [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A prism has a critical angle of 42°. Calculate its refractive index. (1)
(ii) Explain why light entering normally to the long face of a right-angled isosceles prism leaves parallel to its original direction. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) n = 1/sin 42° = 1.49 [B1]
(ii) Light hits each short face at 45° > C, so totally internally reflected [B1]
Two reflections turn it through 180° [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain whether using glass of lower refractive index would allow a larger range of incident angles to be fully reflected in a prism. (2)
questions.solution:
Lower n gives a larger critical angle [B1]
So fewer rays exceed C – the range decreases [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the speed of light in an optical fibre core of refractive index 1.48. (2)
Light gives a second-order maximum at 30° with a grating of 500 lines per mm. Calculate the wavelength. (2)
State how the central maximum changes when a single slit is made narrower. (2)
questions.solution:
Central maximum gets wider [B1]
And dimmer [B1]

questions.prompt: State two properties the two progressive waves forming a stationary wave must share. (2)
questions.solution:
Same frequency / wavelength [B1]
Similar amplitude, travelling in opposite directions [B1]

questions.prompt: A spectral line of wavelength 590 nm has its first-order maximum at 30.0°. Calculate the grating's lines per metre. (3)
Explain whether using the second order or a grating with twice the lines gives a better measurement of a small wavelength difference. (2)
questions.solution:
Both roughly double the angular separation [B1]
Finer grating keeps maxima brighter / fewer overlapping orders – better [B1]

questions.prompt:
A 1.20 m string at 500 Hz shows three loops with antinode amplitude 6.0 mm.
(i) State the amplitude of each progressive wave. (1)
(ii) Calculate the wave speed. (2)
(iii) State the phase relationship of the two waves when all points are at maximum displacement. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 3.0 mm [B1]
(ii) λ = 0.80 m [M1]
v = 400 m s⁻¹ [A1]
(iii) In phase [B1]

questions.prompt: A 10 ns laser pulse has wavelength 600 nm. Calculate the number of wavelengths in the pulse. (2)
Successive resonance positions in an air column are 33 cm apart at 512 Hz. Calculate the speed of sound. (2)

A nylon string (density 1150 kg m⁻³, diameter 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m) with hanging masses 0.50, 0.80 and 1.20 kg vibrates at 110, 140 and 170 Hz.
(i) Show the data fit f ∝ √T. (2)
(ii) Calculate the vibrating length. (3)

(i) Calculate the critical angle for glass of n = 1.6. (1)
(ii) Light in the glass meets a liquid film at 58° and just totally internally reflects. Calculate the liquid's refractive index. (2)
5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m light gives a fourth-order maximum at 30°. Find the lines per mm. (2)

A fibre has core n = 1.47 and cladding n = 1.41.
(i) Calculate the speed of light in the core. (1)
(ii) Calculate the critical angle. (2)
(iii) Calculate the maximum entry angle from air for total internal reflection. (2)
Microwaves (λ ≈ 3 cm) pass through slits 0.12 m apart onto a receiver 0.45 m away. Explain why Young's equation w = λD/s shouldn't be used, and how to find λ. (3)
questions.solution:
Young's equation assumes D ≫ s; here D is only about 4s [B1]
Fringe angles are large, so the approximation fails [B1]
Instead measure path differences of maxima: path difference = nλ [B1]

questions.prompt: The second-order maximum for 650 nm coincides with the third-order maximum for another wavelength. Find it. (1)

Wire A (6.6 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹) and wire B (1.47 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹) are 1.50 m long. Tension is 1.0 N or 5.0 N, and the supply goes up to 50 Hz. Show that only wire B with 1.0 N gives the first five harmonics. (4)
questions.solution:
A at 1.0 N: v = 39 m s⁻¹; f₅ = 65 Hz – too high [M1]
A at 5.0 N and B at 5.0 N give f₅ above 50 Hz too [M1]
B at 1.0 N: v = 26.1 m s⁻¹, f₁ = 8.7 Hz [M1]
f₅ = 43.5 Hz < 50 Hz, so B with 1.0 N [A1]

questions.prompt: 420 nm light hits a grating with slit separation 3.6 μm. Find the total number of maxima. (2)

A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction.
(a) Calculate the acceleration. (3)
(b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2)
(c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. [M1 M1 A1]
(b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. [M1 A1]
(c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: A catapult beam pivots so that a counterweight of 450 kg acts 0.80 m from the pivot. On the other side, a rope holding the beam down and a projectile of weight 180 N both act vertically 2.4 m from the pivot. Calculate the tension in the rope. (4)

The projectile is released horizontally at 16 m/s from 6.0 m above the ground.
(i) Calculate its horizontal range, ignoring air resistance. (2)
(ii) Discuss the effect on range if it were released at an upward angle with the same speed. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) t = √(2 × 6.0 ÷ 9.81) = 1.11 s [M1]
Range = 16 × 1.11 = 18 m [A1]
(ii) Longer time in the air [B1]
But smaller horizontal velocity component; range increases for small angles [B1]

questions.prompt:
A 1200 kg car travelling at 90 km/h hits a barrier at 25° to the barrier.
(i) Show that its kinetic energy is about 380 kJ. (2)
(ii) Calculate the component of its momentum parallel to the barrier. (3)

The momentum parallel to the barrier is unchanged after impact.
(i) Show that about 70 kJ of kinetic energy is lost. (3)
(ii) The barrier exerts an average force of 50 kN at right angles. Deduce whether it moves less than the 1.5 m allowed. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) v = 22.7 m/s [M1]
Ek after = ½ × 1200 × 22.7² = 3.08 × 10⁵ J [M1]
Loss ≈ 6.7 × 10⁴ J [A1]
(ii) s = 6.7 × 10⁴ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁴ = 1.3 m [M1]
Less than 1.5 m so it passes [A1]

questions.prompt: A cylindrical counterweight has diameter 5.0 cm, length 0.20 m and weight 30 N. Deduce whether it is made of concrete (2400 kg m⁻³), iron (7900 kg m⁻³) or brass (8500 kg m⁻³). (3)
A cable with tension 45 N pulls on a gate at 15° to the gate. The point of attachment is 1.1 m from the hinge. Calculate the moment about the hinge. (2)
A car moves at a constant 20 m/s with a driving force of 800 N. Calculate the power and express the watt in base units. (2)
questions.solution:
16 kW [B1]
kg m² s⁻³ [B1]

questions.prompt: Two wires of the same material have lengths L and 2L and diameters d and 2d. Find the ratio of their extensions under the same load. (3)
questions.solution:
x ∝ L/d² [M1]
Second: 2L/4d² = ½ of first [M1]

(ii) Describe how to limit random error in the diameter. (2)
(iii) A rod of diameter 0.76 mm has mass per unit length 3.54 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹. Calculate its density. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 6.48 mm [B1]
(ii) Measure at several points and orientations along the rod [B1]
Calculate the mean [B1]
(iii) A = π × (0.38 × 10⁻³)² = 4.54 × 10⁻⁷ m² [M1]
ρ = 7.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³ [A1]

questions.prompt: Show the SI unit of viscosity η in F = 6πηrv. (1)
questions.solution: N m⁻² s (= Pa s) [B1]

questions.prompt: A steel strip clamped at one end deflects by y when a mass m hangs from its free end, with y ∝ mL³/Ewt³. Describe how to find E graphically using only one strip and masses up to 250 g. (4)
questions.solution:
Keep L fixed and vary m in 50 g steps [B1]
Measure y each time against a vertical ruler [B1]
Measure w and t with a micrometer at several points [B1]
Plot y against m; E is found from the gradient [B1]

questions.prompt: Putty cylinders of constant volume V have resistance R = ρL²/V. Explain how to find ρ graphically and give its unit. (3)
questions.solution:
Plot R against L² [B1]
Gradient = ρ/V so ρ = gradient × V [B1]
Unit Ω m [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a graph of p against 1/V that is a straight line through the origin confirms Boyle's law. (3)
questions.solution:
Straight line through the origin shows p ∝ 1/V [B1]
So pV is constant [B1]
For fixed mass at constant temperature [B1]

questions.prompt: State one property of the trapped air that must be kept constant and how. (2)
questions.solution:
Temperature [B1]
Change pressure slowly and wait before each reading [B1]

questions.prompt: A piston of mass 0.35 kg and area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² rests on trapped air. Calculate the extra pressure due to the piston. (2)
Explain how to read the volume of air above coloured oil in a Boyle's law tube correctly. (2)
questions.solution:
Read from the bottom of the meniscus [B1]
With the eye level with it to avoid parallax [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a current balance with a wire in a uniform field can give B from a graph. (4)
questions.solution:
Wire of known length L in the field, on a top-pan balance [B1]
Record balance reading for increasing current [B1]
Plot force (Δm × g) against I [B1]
Gradient = BL, so B = gradient ÷ L [B1]

questions.prompt: The droop y of a steel tape overhang x is modelled by y = Axⁿ. Explain how to find n and A from a log graph. (3)
questions.solution:
Plot ln y against ln x [B1]
Gradient = n [B1]
Intercept = ln A, so A = e^(intercept) [B1]

questions.prompt: Trapped air has volume 207 cm³ at 20 °C and 255 cm³ at 90 °C. Use Charles's law to estimate absolute zero in °C. (3)
Describe how to measure the volume of water accurately and avoid systematic error. (2)
questions.solution:
Use a measuring cylinder of suitable size [B1]
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of using a data logger to obtain a lamp's I–V characteristic. (2)
questions.solution:
Many readings taken quickly, before the filament changes temperature [B1]
Removes human reading error [B1]

questions.prompt: A lamp rated at 12 V is placed in series with an identical lamp across 12 V. Explain why the total power is more than half the rated power. (3)
questions.solution:
Each lamp gets 6 V [B1]
Cooler filament has lower resistance [B1]
So the current is more than half, giving more than 50% of rated power [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain whether a search coil can measure a steady magnetic field from a d.c. coil. (2)
questions.solution:
A search coil only gives an emf when flux changes [B1]
So unsuitable for a steady field – use a Hall probe [B1]

questions.prompt: A coil is rotated 25° about its centre. Calculate the percentage change in the horizontal field component measured along the original axis. (2)
questions.solution:
B_H × cos 25° = 0.906 B_H [M1]
9.4% decrease [A1]

questions.prompt:
A microwave receiver detects a minimum when direct and reflected waves combine.
(i) State the phase difference. (1)
(ii) Explain why the minimum isn't zero. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) π rad (180°) [B1]
(ii) Reflected wave has smaller amplitude than the direct wave [B1]

questions.prompt: After each rebound n, a glider's distance x decreases. Explain how a graph of ln x against n tests for exponential decrease and gives x at n = 20. (3)
questions.solution:
If x = x₀e^(−kn), ln x = ln x₀ − kn [B1]
Straight line confirms exponential decrease [B1]
Read ln x at n = 20 from the line, then x = e^(ln x) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the time-base should be set so one or two cycles fill the screen when measuring a time constant. (2)
questions.solution:
Larger trace gives smaller percentage uncertainty in readings [B1]
But the whole decay must still be visible [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Background is 630 counts in 15 min. At 530 mm, counts are 90, 117 and 102 in 100 s. Calculate the corrected count rate. (2)
(ii) At 380 mm the corrected rate is 0.76 s⁻¹. Test whether R ∝ 1/d². (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Background = 0.70 s⁻¹; mean = 1.03 s⁻¹ [M1]
Corrected = 0.33 s⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) Rd²: 0.33 × 0.530² = 0.093; 0.76 × 0.380² = 0.110 [M1]
Similar (within uncertainty), so roughly inverse square [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) At 100 s⁻¹, about 2 photons per second are missed. Calculate the dead time. (1)
(ii) Explain why a detector with 0.01 s dead time can't catch all 100 s⁻¹ photons. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) td = 0.02 ÷ 100 = 2 × 10⁻⁴ s [B1]
(ii) Decay is random, so photons don't arrive evenly [B1]
Some arrive within 0.01 s of each other and are missed [B1]

questions.prompt:
Five half-life readings are 12.00, 11.94, 12.06, 12.04 and 12.16 s.
(i) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
(ii) Show the time constant is about 17 s. (1)
Explain the use of the mirror behind an analogue meter's pointer. (2)
questions.solution:
Line up the pointer with its reflection [B1]
Ensures eye is perpendicular to the scale, avoiding parallax error [B1]

questions.prompt: log(R/Ω) = −0.772 log(E/lx) + 5.09. Calculate R at 130 lx. (2)
Illuminance follows E = 400e^(−μN) with μ = 0.090. Find the minimum number of slides to halve E. (2)
In M = kBI + nZ + Y, M is a mass. Find the base units of k. (3)
questions.solution:
T = kg s⁻² A⁻¹ [M1]
k = kg ÷ (kg s⁻² A⁻¹ × A) [M1]
= s² [A1]

questions.prompt: Outline how error bars are used to find the uncertainty in a gradient. (2)
questions.solution:
Draw the steepest/shallowest line through all error bars [B1]
Uncertainty = difference between worst and best gradients [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why 20 periods are timed rather than one. (1)
(ii) 20T readings are 19.22, 18.91, 19.36, 19.04 and 19.45 s. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in T. (2)
(iii) State why readings are repeated. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Reduces percentage uncertainty from reaction time [B1]
(ii) Mean = 19.20 s; ± 0.27 s [M1]
1.4% [A1]
(iii) To identify anomalies and reduce random error [B1]

questions.prompt: For a floating test tube, T ∝ 1/√ρ. T = 0.587 s in oil (849 kg m⁻³) and 0.534 s in milk. Calculate the density of milk. (2)

(i) Explain chromatic aberration in a refracting telescope. (2)
(ii) State the shapes of the primary and secondary mirrors in a Cassegrain telescope. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Different wavelengths refract by different amounts [B1]
So they focus at different points, giving coloured fringes [B1]
(ii) Primary concave, secondary convex [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the minimum angular resolution of a 39 m optical telescope at 500 nm and a 100 m radio telescope at 21 cm, and state which gives the more detailed image. (4)
questions.solution:
Optical: 500 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ 39 = 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ rad [M1]
Radio: 0.21 ÷ 100 = 2.1 × 10⁻³ rad [M1]
Optical resolution is much smaller [B1]
So the optical telescope gives more detail [A1]

questions.prompt: A star has apparent magnitude 0.40 and absolute magnitude 2.70. Calculate its distance and give the unit. (3)
State and explain which spectral class has the strongest hydrogen Balmer absorption lines. (2)
questions.solution:
Class A [B1]
Temperature about 10 000 K gives many hydrogen atoms with electrons in n = 2 [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the radial velocity method for detecting exoplanets. (2)
questions.solution:
Star orbits common centre of mass with the planet [B1]
Periodic Doppler shift of the star's spectral lines [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the evolution of a Sun-like star on the HR diagram from main sequence to white dwarf. (3)
questions.solution:
Moves off the main sequence to the red giant region (top right) [B1]
Loses outer layers as a planetary nebula [B1]
Core becomes a white dwarf (bottom left) [B1]

questions.prompt: Galaxy P has z = 5.0 × 10⁻³ at 7.0 × 10⁷ ly; galaxy Q has z = 2.5 × 10⁻³ at 3.4 × 10⁷ ly. Discuss whether these data are consistent with Hubble's law. (3)
questions.solution:
v = zc, so v ∝ z [B1]
z ratio = 2.0; distance ratio = 2.06 [M1]
Approximately proportional, so consistent [A1]

questions.prompt: State one problem in determining the distance to a quasar. (2)
questions.solution:
Quasars aren't standard candles / luminosity unknown [B1]
Distance relies on redshift and Hubble's law, uncertain H₀ [B1]

questions.prompt: A refracting telescope in normal adjustment has lens separation 15.0 m and angular magnification 600. Calculate the focal length of the eyepiece. (3)
Compare using a CCD with the naked eye for observing faint binary stars. (3)
questions.solution:
CCD quantum efficiency ~80% vs eye ~1% [B1]
CCD can integrate light over long exposures [B1]
Eye has a slightly better resolution limit but CCD gives a permanent image [B1]

questions.prompt:
A spectral line of laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm from an eclipsing binary varies between 656.72 nm and 655.94 nm.
(i) Explain why the average differs from the laboratory value. (1)
(ii) Calculate the orbital speed of the star. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) The binary system as a whole is receding [B1]
(ii) Δλ = (656.72 − 655.94) ÷ 2 = 0.39 nm [M1]
v = 0.39 ÷ 656.28 × 3.0 × 10⁸ [M1]
= 1.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: The star orbits at 1.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ with a period of 2.5 days. Calculate its orbital radius. (2)

A quasar has apparent magnitude 13.0 at 600 Mpc.
(i) Show that its absolute magnitude is about −26. (2)
(ii) A galaxy has absolute magnitude −22.9. Calculate how many times brighter the quasar would be at the same distance. (3)
A black hole has mass 1.0 × 10⁴² kg. Calculate the average density within its event horizon. (3)
Discuss how cosmic microwave background radiation supports the Big Bang theory, including a calculation of its temperature from a peak wavelength of 1.06 mm. (4)
questions.solution:
Radiation arrives from all directions with a black-body spectrum [B1]
T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1.06 × 10⁻³ = 2.7 K [M1 A1]
Predicted as radiation from the hot early universe, redshifted by expansion [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Define the parsec. (1)
(ii) Rigel has apparent magnitude 0.12 and absolute magnitude −7.8. Calculate its distance. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond [B1]
(ii) 7.92 = 5 log(d/10) [M1]
d = 380 pc [A1]

questions.prompt: State the spectral class of a star with surface temperature 12 000 K. (1)
questions.solution: B [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Star A (m = 6.0) is 40 times brighter than star B. Calculate the apparent magnitude of B. (2)
(ii) An eye with 7 mm pupil sees down to m = 6.0. Deduce whether B is visible with a 60 mm telescope. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) m = 6.0 + 2.5 log 40 [M1]
= 10.0 [A1]
(ii) Gain = (60/7)² = 73, i.e. 4.7 magnitudes [M1]
Limit 10.7 > 10.0, so visible [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain two ways a CCD helps observe dim stars. (3)
questions.solution:
High quantum efficiency (~80%) captures most photons [B1]
Can integrate over long exposures [B1]
Digital image can be processed / stacked [B1]

questions.prompt: A star orbiting a black hole edge-on shows a line varying between 374.96 nm and 373.53 nm. Calculate its orbital speed. (3)
Compare the resolution of a radio array 1.3 × 10⁷ m across at 1.3 mm with a 2.4 m optical telescope at 410 nm. (2)
questions.solution:
Array: 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ rad; optical: 1.7 × 10⁻⁷ rad [M1]
Array resolves much finer detail [A1]

questions.prompt: State what type Ia supernova observations showed about expansion and the explanation proposed. (2)
questions.solution:
Expansion of the universe is accelerating [B1]
Attributed to dark energy [B1]

questions.prompt: Two nearby stars have temperatures 6000 K and 4700 K. Compare their colours and explain how magnitudes can test whether they form a binary. (3)
questions.solution:
Hotter star is whiter/yellower; cooler is orange/redder [B1]
A binary is at one distance [B1]
So m difference should equal M difference [B1]

questions.prompt:
A telescope in normal adjustment has angular magnification 75 and eyepiece focal length 22 mm.
(i) Calculate the lens separation. (2)
(ii) Jupiter's image subtends 1.7 × 10⁻² rad. Its radius is 7.0 × 10⁴ km. Calculate Jupiter's distance. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) fo = 75 × 22 = 1650 mm [M1]
Separation = 1.67 m [A1]
(ii) Angle without telescope = 2.27 × 10⁻⁴ rad [M1]
d = 1.4 × 10⁵ km ÷ 2.27 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.2 × 10⁸ km [A1]

questions.prompt: A star with T = 6.0 × 10³ K has radius 9.6 × 10⁶ m. Calculate its power. (2)
Calculate the Schwarzschild radius of a 1.60 × 10⁸ solar-mass black hole (M☉ = 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and state its unit. (3)
Theta Carinae has 5 times the Sun's radius and T = 31 000 K (Sun 5800 K). Calculate the orbital radius at which a planet receives Earth's power per m². (4)
Galaxy IC2497 has redshift 0.0516. Calculate its distance (H₀ = 65 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹). (3)
Explain the Rayleigh criterion. (2)
questions.solution:
Two images are just resolved [B1]
When the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other [B1]

questions.prompt: M87 is 5.3 × 10⁷ ly away. Calculate its recession velocity (H₀ = 65 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, 1 pc = 3.26 ly). (3)
Aa1 has M = −5.4 and m = 2.5; Aa2 has M = −2.9 and m = 5.0. Show they could be a binary system. (3)
questions.solution:
Aa1: m − M = 7.9 [M1]
Aa2: m − M = 7.9 [M1]
Same distance, consistent with a binary [A1]

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse's intensity rose from I to 1.15I at constant temperature. It was 548 ly away with radius 700 R☉. Test group X (distance is really 530 ly) and group Y (radius is really 750 R☉). (3)
questions.solution:
New d = 548 ÷ √1.15 = 511 ly, so X's 530 ly isn't enough [M1]
New R = 700 × √1.15 = 751 R☉ [M1]
Y's claim is consistent [A1]

questions.prompt: Compare the image brightness of a 70 mm refractor and a 400 mm reflector. (2)
questions.solution:
Ratio = (400/70)² [M1]
Reflector is about 33 times brighter [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Calculate the temperature of a black body peaking at 1.0 μm. (1)
(ii) Sarin (23 pc) has apparent magnitude 3.1. Calculate its absolute magnitude. (2)
Kornephoros (43 pc) and Rutilicus (11 pc) are both class G with apparent magnitude 2.8. Deduce which is larger. (3)
questions.solution:
Same apparent brightness, so L ∝ d²: Kornephoros 15 times more luminous [M1]
Same class means same temperature [M1]
L ∝ R², so Kornephoros is about 4 times larger [A1]

questions.prompt:
A refractor has a 305 mm objective of focal length 5.03 m.
(i) Find the wavelength for a resolution of 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ rad. (2)
(ii) The eye resolves 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ rad. Find the eyepiece focal length needed to just resolve 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ rad. (3)
Markarian-231 is 5.81 × 10⁸ ly away with z = 0.0415. Estimate the age of the Universe in seconds. (4)
Explain the cosmic microwave background and how it supports the Big Bang. (3)
questions.solution:
Radiation from when the Universe became transparent [B1]
Stretched to microwave wavelengths by expansion (≈ 2.7 K black body) [B1]
Uniform in all directions – predicted by the Big Bang [B1]

questions.prompt:
A driver's unaided far point is 60 cm.
(i) Name the defect. (1)
(ii) Calculate the power of the lens needed to see distant objects. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Myopia [B1]
(ii) Object at infinity, image at −0.60 m [M1]
P = 1/f = −1/0.60 [M1]
= −1.7 D [A1]

questions.prompt:
A loudspeaker gives intensity 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² at 10 m.
(i) Calculate the intensity at 6.0 m. (2)
(ii) Two listeners hear 70 dB and 45 dB. Calculate the ratio of intensities. (2)
Explain how electrons striking a tungsten target produce continuous and characteristic X-ray spectra. (4)
questions.solution:
Electrons decelerate in the target, emitting bremsstrahlung [B1]
Range of decelerations gives a continuous spectrum [B1]
Electrons knock out inner-shell electrons [B1]
Outer electrons fall into vacancies emitting photons of specific energies [B1]

questions.prompt: An A-scan echo from the back of the eye returns 30 μs after the pulse. Ultrasound speed in the eye is 1550 m s⁻¹. Calculate the eye length. (3)
questions.solution:
Distance = 1550 × 30 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.0465 m [M1]
Halve for return path [M1]
l = 2.3 cm [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a B-scan rather than an A-scan is used to guide a needle in amniocentesis. (3)
questions.solution:
A-scan gives only depth along one line [B1]
B-scan builds a 2D image from many lines [B1]
Real-time imaging shows needle and foetus positions [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how age-related hearing loss and noise-induced hearing loss affect the frequency response of the ear. (2)
questions.solution:
Age: reduced sensitivity mainly at high frequencies [B1]
Noise: reduced sensitivity around specific frequencies (about 4 kHz) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A +4.0 D lens corrects an eye condition. Name it. (1)
(ii) An object is 0.60 m from the lens. Calculate the magnification. (3)
X-rays of intensity 0.013 W m⁻² fall on a bone of diameter 0.040 m (μ = 58.3 m⁻¹) over a beam area of 1.0 × 10⁻³ m² for 0.80 s. Estimate the energy absorbed by the bone. (4)
Calculate the intensity of a sound of intensity level 30 dB (I₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻²). (2)
Describe how data for an equal loudness curve are obtained. (2)
questions.solution:
Listener compares tones of different frequencies with a 1 kHz reference [B1]
Adjusts intensity until each sounds equally loud [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) State the purpose of the strong magnetic field in an MR scanner. (1)
(ii) Describe the role of the radio-frequency pulses. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Aligns the spins of hydrogen nuclei [B1]
(ii) RF pulses at the Larmor frequency excite protons out of alignment [B1]
As they relax they emit RF signals that are detected to form the image [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare CT, MRI and ultrasound for imaging calcium kidney stones. (3)
questions.solution:
CT gives clear images of dense stones but a high radiation dose [B1]
MRI has no ionising radiation but stones (no water) show poorly; expensive [B1]
Ultrasound is cheap and safe but lower resolution – CT usually recommended [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain one advantage of a beta source over a gamma source placed next to a tumour. (2)
questions.solution:
Beta has a short range in tissue [B1]
Irradiates the tumour without damaging distant healthy tissue [B1]

questions.prompt: Two dark pixels separated by a light one must not be resolved at 0.50 m. Cones are 1.5 μm across and the eye is 21 mm long. Estimate the minimum pixel line density. (3)
questions.solution:
Images must fall less than 2 cones (3.0 μm) apart: angle = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 0.021 = 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ rad [M1]
Separation at screen = 7.1 × 10⁻⁵ m = 2 pixels [M1]
Pixel width 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ m, about 280 pixels per cm [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why fine detail can't be resolved in dim light. (2)
questions.solution:
In dim light rods are used, not cones [B1]
Many rods share one nerve fibre, so resolution is poor [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Define intensity. (1)
(ii) Pressure at the oval window is 20 times that at the eardrum. Areas are 5.9 × 10⁻⁶ m² and 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ m². Calculate the force ratio. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Power per unit area [B1]
(ii) 20 × 5.9 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ [M1]
= 1.6 [A1]

questions.prompt: State the change in intensity level when the intensity doubles. (1)
questions.solution: Increases by 3 dB [B1]

questions.prompt: A Doppler trace shows blood flow peaks 0.80 s apart. Calculate the heart rate. (2)
questions.solution:
60 ÷ 0.80 [M1]
75 beats per minute [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why gel is used under ECG electrodes and how the skin is prepared. (3)
questions.solution:
Gel is a good conductor, making good electrical contact [B1]
Reduces impedance between skin and electrode [B1]
Skin is cleaned / dead skin and hair removed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a barium meal improves the X-ray image of the stomach. (2)
questions.solution:
Barium has a high atomic number and strongly attenuates X-rays [B1]
Stomach outline appears clearly against soft tissue [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A person's far point is 6.0 m. Name the defect. (1)
(ii) Calculate the power of the correcting lens. (2)
A crowd produces 110 dB. The crowd is reduced by 60%. Estimate the new level. (2)

(i) F-18 has a physical half-life of 110 min. Calculate the percentage left after 4.0 h. (3)
(ii) In PET, detector A registers a photon 0.79 ns before B. Find the source's distance from the midpoint. (2)
questions.solution:

(½)^2.18 = 0.22 [M1]
22% [A1]
(ii) Path difference = 3.0 × 10⁸ × 0.79 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.24 m [M1]
0.12 m from the midpoint towards A [A1]

questions.prompt: Ultrasound passes from muscle (ρ = 1100 kg m⁻³, c = 1600 m s⁻¹) into bone (Z = 5.3 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹). Calculate the percentage transmitted. (3)
questions.solution:
Z_muscle = 1.76 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ [M1]
R = (3.54/7.06)² = 0.25 [M1]
75% transmitted [A1]

questions.prompt: I-131 has physical half-life 8.0 days and biological half-life 66 days. A patient starts at 3.2 GBq and can leave below 1.1 GBq. Deduce whether they can leave after 10 days. (4)
Calculate the intensity level 12 m from a 17 W point source. (3)
An X-ray focal spot 1.0 mm wide is 1.0 m above the plate. The blurred edge must be no more than 0.10 mm. Find the maximum bone-to-plate distance. (2)
A +2.0 D lens is used to view an object 24 cm away. Calculate the image distance. (3)
0.0625% of ultrasound intensity reflects at a blood (1.64 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹) to aorta-wall boundary, where the wall has higher impedance. Calculate the wall's impedance. (4)

(i) Show the effective half-life is about 70 min (physical 110 min, biological 185 min). (1)
(ii) State the range of time differences a PET scanner must measure across a 0.2 m head. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Te = 110 × 185 ÷ 295 = 69 min [B1]
(ii) Maximum = 0.2 ÷ 3 × 10⁸ = 7 × 10⁻¹⁰ s [M1]
Range 0 to about 0.7 ns [A1]

questions.prompt: A fibre core has n = 1.6 and a critical angle of 75° at the cladding. Calculate the cladding's refractive index. (2)
Two points 12 mm apart are 61 m from the eye; the retina is 21 mm behind the lens and cones are 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m wide. Deduce whether they can be resolved. (3)
questions.solution:
θ = 0.012 ÷ 61 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ rad [M1]
Image separation = 0.021 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.1 × 10⁻⁶ m [M1]
More than two cone widths (an unstimulated cone between), so resolved [A1]

questions.prompt: A 7.8 W drill acts as a point source. The safe limit is 110 dB and barriers are 2.0 m away. Deduce whether this is safe. (3)
questions.solution:
I = 0.10 W m⁻² [M1]
r = √(7.8 ÷ (4π × 0.10)) = 2.5 m [M1]
More than 2.0 m, so barriers aren't far enough [A1]

questions.prompt: Lead has half-value thickness 4.2 × 10⁻³ m and density 1.1 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³. Calculate the mass attenuation coefficient and give its unit. (3)
State three ways to limit healthy tissue's exposure during X-ray imaging. (3)
questions.solution:
Collimate the beam to the area of interest [B1]
Aluminium filter removes low-energy photons [B1]
Short exposure / intensifying screens / shielding [B1]

questions.prompt:
A fly-press's rotating parts store 12 J when rotating at 3.0 rev s⁻¹.
(i) Calculate their moment of inertia. (2)
(ii) They are brought uniformly to rest in 0.10 s. Calculate the angular deceleration and angle turned. (3)
Each ball (radius R) is a distance y from the axis. Deduce whether increasing y by 15% or increasing R by 15% gives the greater increase in stored energy (treat balls as point masses). (3)
questions.solution:
